newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Western grid outages pit fish against power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Western grid outages pit fish against power.

text.p: Operators of the western U.S. electricity grid, struggling to devise a fail-safe plan to keep the lights on following two big blackouts this summer, are running up against a major environmental hurdle.
At issue is whether protecting fish, like the endangered chinook salmon, is always more important than producing power.

Randy Hardy, the top official at the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), recently argued power dispatchers on the Columbia River should be given unilateral authority to suspend fish-related flow requirements during power emergencies.

BPA is the federal agency that markets power produced at U.S. Northwest hydroelectric dams, mainly on the Columbia and Snake Rivers in Idaho, Washington, and Oregon -- historically some of the best salmon rivers in the country.

Bonneville agreed in 1995 to a draft "biological opinion" from the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), identifying efforts to restore the rivers' fish stocks as their number two priority after flood control.
Power generation dropped to third place on the list.
Using NMFS guidelines, BPA is diverting more water from hydroturbines so fewer fish are mutiliated as they swim downstream and river levels are kept high enough for spawning.
But environmentalists, backed by the Endangered Species Act, continue to push for stricter adherance to the NMFS's standards amid concerns those standards might be undermined.

"Whenever there is a gray area, the power system seems to get the benefit of the doubt rather than the fish...It should be the other way around," said Tim Stearns, executive director of Save Our Wild Salmon (SOS) a Seattle-based coalition of environmentalists and recreation groups.

SOS was dismayed when BPA, after consulting the NMFS, halted fish-related spills for three days at The Dalles dam on the Columbia River in a bid to stabilize voltage on the grid after the huge August 10 power outage.
BPA estimated some 2,000 fish were killed by the decision.
"We might have had another outage," if action had not been taken to boost Northwest power generation, BPA's Hardy said.
But Stearns noted "fish didn't choose to be part of the hydro system. You can't divide them from it. There needs to be an orderly process defining when fish can be used to back-up the power system."
The grid's limits are increasingly tested as deregulation of the electricity market puts more pressure on it to carry heavier loads over greater distances than ever before.
Heavy loads on lines from Northwest hydroelectric dams to California were a key factor in the July 2 and August 10 outages, which hit millions of customers in several states.

BPA's move August 11 to crank up power output at the expense of the fish was taken to stabilize voltage on the grid and avoid even wider outages during a week when hot weather in California was pushing air-conditioning demand to new highs.
"California utilities said they didn't ask Bonneville to kill fish, but effectively that's what they did," said Stearns, referring to the August 11 plea for more power.
To help speed decision-making in an emergency, BPA's Hardy called for studies to determine who should have the final authority to suspend spills or other fish-related measures.
He also said environmentalists and fish advocates need to be consulted on how to compensate for the impact of such disruptions.
But Jim Baker, Northwest salmon campaign coordinator for the Sierra Club, said this should never become an issue.
"If the situation has reached a point where only micro-management of the dam system will keep the lights on, something is drastically wrong," he said.
